summary: Lists requirements for a new IETF tool that Area Directors would use to create, re-charter, and close working groups, and that the wider community could use to see how chartering is going. It is input for later design work, not a protocol, and is informational only.

eli5.summary: Before building a tool, you write down what it must do. This is that wish list for a program that helps the people running IETF groups start, change, and finish those groups, and lets everyone see the progress.

subtitle: A wish list for a web tool that would let IETF Area Directors create, change and close working groups.

tldr.problem: Creating, rechartering and closing IETF working groups was done almost entirely by hand: an Area Director sent a message to the Secretariat's ticket system, and Secretariat staff updated databases, agendas and announcements manually.
tldr.mechanism: The document lists requirements for a Datatracker tool: a record for each working group, a set of review states for chartering and rechartering, charter ballots, a way to request closure, and public search, comparison and Atom feeds.
tldr.outcome: It is input for a later design and development effort, and it says it may be used to issue an RFP. It does not define a protocol.

today: RFC 6292 is an Informational document that has been updated by RFC 6433. It is a requirements list for a tool, not a protocol.

sections.title: The Manual Charter Process
sections.content:
RFC 2418 describes how IETF working groups (WGs) are formed and run. Since it was published in 1998, the IETF has started and shut down many dozen WGs, and many WGs have had dozens of charter changes.

According to the document, virtually all of this work was done manually. An Area Director (AD) sends a message to the Secretariat's ticket system. A member of the Secretariat staff then updates the internal Secretariat database and the IETF Datatracker, places the WG on the IESG teleconference agenda when appropriate, and sends out all the required messages.

The IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC) asked for a better tool, and this document was prepared at its request. When complete, the document may be used to issue an RFP for the design and development of the tool. Creation and rechartering involve internal review by the IESG and IAB, external review by the community and other standards bodies, and likely approval of a final charter by the IESG. Closing a WG does not require IESG review or approval. Milestone changes are not part of the charter process described here.
sections.eli5: Right now people send notes to each other and copy information by hand every time a group starts, changes or stops. The wish list describes a tool that would do the copying for them.

sections.title: WG Records, Comments and Charter Names
sections.content:
The tool holds a WG record for each new WG being considered and for every WG whose charter is under review. A record has fields such as the WG name and acronym, chairs, secretary, technical advisors, shepherding AD, IETF area, charter text, mailing list, other web sites, earlier acronyms and the reason for chartering. It also holds the state in the review process, annotated as either a proposed WG or an existing WG being rechartered.

Any AD can edit fields and change the review state. The normal order of steps is shown, but an AD can set the state to any valid value at any time. The Secretariat can do anything an AD can do in the tool. Any AD can add a comment to a record under review, flagged as blocking or non-blocking.

Charter text proposals are kept for history in files named charter-ietf-wgacronym-nn[-mm], where nn is a two-digit charter number starting at 00 before the first charter and mm is a two-digit proposal number. ADs can also view and edit the standard "WG Review" and "WG Action" announcements before they go out.
sections.eli5: Each group gets a file card with its name, leaders and goals. Every draft of its goals is saved with a number, like keeping every version of a homework essay.

sections.title: Chartering a New WG
sections.content:
Any AD can create a new WG record with a simple web form. Creating it succeeds as long as no other WG has the same name, and the tool warns the AD if the proposed acronym was used in earlier charter proposals. The WG chairs may be left off at first. The record starts in the state Informal IESG review, and the AD proposes an internal review time in weeks, with a default of one week. The tool should prompt the AD who tries to move on sooner than that.

The states are: Informal IESG review, Internal review (the IESG and IAB look at the early draft), External review (the IETF community and possibly other standards organizations look at it), IESG review, WG exists and Not currently under review. Moving into several states sends a note to the Secretariat, for example to place the item on the next IESG telechat or to send the external review announcement. The AD can choose whether the announcement also goes to other standards bodies, and the default is that it does.

The document notes that some Secretariat tools truncated acronyms longer than eight characters, so the new tool should have a configuration setting that starts at 8.
sections.eli5: A new group has to pass through several checkpoints, like a school club that needs approval from the teachers, then feedback from the students, then a final yes.

sections.title: Rechartering, Ballots and Closing
sections.content:
To recharter a WG, an AD uses a web form that shows the current charter and lets every field be edited. The states mirror the ones for new WGs, but each is prefixed with WG exists, for example WG exists; Informal IESG recharter review, and they carry the annotation Rechartering. The IESG decides whether a recharter needs external review, and many do not. Chartering involves two IESG telechats and rechartering one or two.

The tool needs a new ballot facility for charter approval, since the Datatracker only had ballots for Internet-Drafts. ADs can express yes, no or abstain, and can change their positions over time.

An AD can also ask the Secretariat to close a WG. The request prompts for what to do with each active Internet-Draft (withdraw it, move it to another WG, convert it to an individual submission and so on), the wording of the closure announcement, and whether the WG mailing list stays open.
sections.eli5: Changing a group's goals follows the same checkpoints as starting one. Closing a group means saying what happens to its unfinished work and whether its chat room stays open.

sections.title: Searching and Tracking Charters
sections.content:
Everyone in the IETF community can view the public part of the charter database, which should explain the states. They can search by WG name, acronym, charter state, shepherding AD, area, text in any field or earlier acronyms. They can also view snapshots of earlier charter versions, which include area, AD, name, acronym, chairs and charter text.

The tool must make it easy to compare versions of proposed charter wording, up to and including the approved version, and to compare two approved charters. It must also compare versions that carry different acronyms if the acronym changed during chartering.

Finally, the tool has to provide an Atom feed (RFC 4287) for charter changes. Each entry holds the full WG record plus an indication of what changed since the previous entry. The tool is to be initialized with records for WGs already in progress and with as much current and historical data as can be loaded in a mostly automated way.
sections.eli5: Anyone can look up a group, see how its goals changed over time, and subscribe to get a ping whenever something changes.

sections.title: Access and Security
sections.content: Area Directors and the IETF Secretariat already had access to perform some Datatracker actions that other community members do not, and this access control continues to be used in many of the extensions. The document says that creating a new tool for tracking WG charters does not affect the security of the Internet in any significant fashion.
sections.eli5: Only the grown-ups in charge can change the records, while everybody else can just read them.
